questions.question: Explain what radiation is and how it differs from conduction and convection, using the example of the Sun heating the Earth.
questions.expected_answer: Radiation is the transfer of heat as invisible (infrared) waves that travel in straight lines and need no particles, so it can pass through a vacuum. Conduction needs particles in contact (mainly solids) and convection needs a moving fluid (liquid or gas). The space between the Sun and Earth is almost empty, so the Sun's energy can only reach Earth by radiation.

questions.question: Describe a fair test to show which surface absorbs radiant heat better, a dull black one or a shiny one, and state the expected result.
questions.expected_answer: Use two identical cans with the same amount of water at the same starting temperature; paint one dull black and cover the other with shiny foil; put a thermometer in each; place both the same distance from a lamp or in the same sunlight; record temperatures every few minutes. Only the surface is changed. The black can warms faster because dark, dull surfaces absorb radiation well, while shiny surfaces reflect it.

questions.question: Explain how a solar cooker uses ideas about radiation to cook food.
questions.expected_answer: Shiny reflectors and foil-lined walls reflect sunlight onto the pot; the pot is painted dull black so it absorbs the radiation well and heats up; a clear lid lets sunlight in but slows heat escaping and stops warm air leaving by convection; insulated walls slow conduction. The trapped heat builds up enough to cook food without fuel.
